name: Uma Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What happened at work this morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma Varga, forty-three, and I spent the first hour matching a childcare centre's relief-worker shifts to its payroll sheet. I prepare accounts and tax returns at Elm Court Accounts, and I like the call when a centre manager finally understands why a wage total changed. I dislike the late payroll list that arrives after the return is nearly signed. I have a bachelor's in accounting and a professional accountancy qualification, with years of ordinary experience rather than a specialist title.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you use the tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Owen works on an ambulance, our children are eight and twelve, and the mortgage is well within our budget while both wages continue. Elm Court pays me above the usual rate because I handle several large centres, and we have nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other accounting firms nearby. I use an AI drafting tool now and then after a colleague proves it works, but I check every total against the signed shift sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A modest sorter would be useful if it stops us entering the same wage line twice. I use a drafting tool now and then after my colleague tests it, but I still read the signed payroll sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the childcare centres a quick draft is not a checked return. I'd say at work that a saved hour should go toward answering the manager's questions, not just closing a file faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our household feels secure in this picture. I'm forty-three, experienced with childcare-centre accounts and paid above the usual rate because I handle several large centres. Owen's ambulance wage is steady, we have nine months saved, and there are plenty of similar firms near our mortgaged home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the signed payroll sheets beside each centre return and use only the tested draft tool. I'd keep adding two hundred a month from pay to our emergency account. In the first year of a plateau I'd leave the children's swimming lessons in place and ask for a quieter day to answer client questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the bills. The work can wear me out, but I do not see my paid hours changing here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the signed sheet catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A centre manager sent a wage total that included the same relief worker twice. The AI payroll draft showed two relief shifts, but the signed sheet had only one. I found the duplicate before the tax return went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep swimming lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Swimming is the one hour our children are both happy in the same pool. We can pay for it with current wages. If our emergency account began to fall, we'd review the extras then, not before.

say: I would keep **signed payroll checks** behind every quick client draft.
I would use saved time for **client questions**.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and two wages feel stable.
I expect **paid hours** to stay steady in a plateau.
do: Keep **signed centre payroll sheets** beside every tested client draft.
Deposit **two hundred monthly** from pay into emergency savings.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and bills.
S0.quote: The AI payroll draft showed two relief shifts, but the signed sheet had only one.
fieldNote: A **duplicate relief shift** is the concrete reason she keeps paper payroll checks beside AI drafts.
Her **nine-month cushion** and two wages allow swimming to stay in the budget.

steps.text: Keep signed payroll sheets beside tested centre tax drafts
Deposit two hundred monthly from pay into emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing to centre managers and checking wage lists are most of my week. If a tool does both quickly, the firm could shrink our review rota even if the client still needs someone to answer a question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see a tested error report before we let the tool send letters. I'd tell colleagues the hours saved and the people affected should be on the same page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own week could lose a day when the next contract renews. Nine months saved gives us time to look, but Owen's ambulance shifts vary around school holidays and my higher pay supports the mortgage. There are plenty of firms nearby, though some may cut the same checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid pilot on fifteen completed childcare-centre returns after another firm has shown the tool works. I'd compare its wage flags with signed shifts and put errors in a note for our manager. If my days are cut, I'd apply for a posted education-finance job only with written mortgage-covering pay, a confirmed start and school pickup that Owen or a club can actually cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own income, though I can test before acting. I would rather count errors than guess whether a manager likes the new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would cover pickup for a new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen sometimes works a late ambulance run and cannot promise Thursday pickup. I'd ask the after-school club for a confirmed place before accepting any new shift. An advertised salary looks different after care fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partner refuses paid pilot hours, I would keep the current checks and not train on live client files at night. I'd still ask for the staffing plan in writing. I need to know when a day might go.

say: I would request a **tested error report** before software sends letters to centre managers.
I would show **saved hours and staffing** together.
think: My **review day** could disappear when the next large childcare contract renews.
Our **reserve** buys time, but not my higher wage.
do: Pilot **fifteen centre returns** on approved paid time, comparing wage flags with signed shifts and reporting errors to the manager.
Keep **current payroll checks** if pilot funding is refused.
Apply for **posted education finance** after cuts only with written mortgage pay, signed start and confirmed childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a lost paid day.
S1.quote: An advertised salary looks different after care fees.
fieldNote: She waits for a **proven tool** and checks wage flags against signed shifts.
The **education job** requires written mortgage pay, confirmed start and childcare that covers ambulance shifts.

steps.text: Pilot proven checker on fifteen centre returns during paid time; compare signed shifts and report errors
Keep signed payroll checks if paid pilot is refused
Apply after day cut for posted education job if written mortgage wage, start, pickup fit
Request written staffing plan if paid pilot funding is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too soon for centres to decide who answers a wrong tax notice. If full AGI does our thinking work cheaply, the firm might stop paying an accountant to check a payroll sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staffing plan and notice, and I'd support a temporary wage bridge. I'd still want centre managers to know which person can answer if an automated return is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accounts job to end in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. My work is desk thinking, so robots around 2031 do not delay that loss. Owen's hands-on ambulance work may hold longer, but robots later could change it too, and nine months saved is not a permanent income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payment now and hold three hundred a month in cash. I'd check the posted hospital finance vacancies, but I would leave this job only for a funded offer with written pay covering the mortgage, a signed start and confirmed pickup. In the first year after 2028, if my firm cuts me, I'd claim wage support while using the reserve for ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a high wage. A nine-month buffer can run down quickly if two workplaces change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner work more hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen's next two months of ambulance shifts are on the rota; we would count those, not possible extra nights. I'd tell the children the family trip can wait, but I wouldn't cancel their swimming without a real loss. We can make a budget from confirmed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would hospital finance be protected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hospital finance post is still screen work, so I would call it a bridge. If no funded opening is posted, I stay on paid centre accounts and look elsewhere. I won't trade a wage for a hospital logo.

say: I would seek **notice** and a **wage bridge** before account jobs vanish.
I would ask who **answers tax errors** after automation.
think: My **desk job** could end soon after 2028 despite years of centre work.
Owen’s **hands-on work** may last longer, not forever.
do: Hold **three hundred monthly** instead of extra mortgage payments.
Leave only for a **funded hospital offer** with written pay, start and pickup.
Claim **wage support** after 2028 loss; if no hospital vacancy, retain available paid centre accounts and look elsewhere.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a high wage.
S2.quote: I won't trade a wage for a hospital logo.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her accounts desk in 2028 before robots might affect ambulance work.
A **hospital post** is a bridge requiring funded salary, signed start and confirmed childcare.

steps.text: Hold three hundred monthly in cash instead of extra mortgage payments
Take funded hospital finance offer only with mortgage wage, signed start and confirmed pickup
Claim wage support after 2028 accounts job loss
Keep available paid centre accounts and seek other posted work if no funded hospital opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to test whether centres want help explaining payroll to their staff, not just sending a tax form. I would still expect the routine checking to shrink when AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to publish an actual fee for staff-pay meetings before calling it a new service. I'd want both the centre and our firm to agree on who checks the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could sit with centre managers and explain why a relief worker's wage changed. AI may calculate it by 2031, but a person might still help with a hard conversation. Robots around 2034 do not extend my tax-checking desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our partner to fund one supervised pay-explanation meeting a month for three centres, learning to lead it on my normal paid day. I'd keep their returns while we see whether the centres pay again at a fee covering my time. In the first year after 2031, if routine tax hours end, I'd stay on paid meetings only if two centres renew; otherwise I'd apply for a posted centre-finance officer role with written mortgage pay and a confirmed start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can ask three existing clients instead of guessing. I won't call a thank-you a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in a pay meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One centre manager once had to explain a missed allowance to a worker. I could help trace the wage line, but I'd want my supervisor to check the numbers before anyone is told what they are owed. The person matters more than a neat letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner refuses paid meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partner will not fund the meetings, I'd keep my current tax files and leave the idea alone. I would not do free evening sessions for a service the firm hopes to sell. A new job would need an actual posted opening.

I would keep a **named figure checker** for staff pay.
think: A **person-led meeting** might still earn a fee from centres handling wage questions.
My **routine tax checks** remain exposed in 2031.
do: Learn **monthly pay meetings** for three centres under paid supervisor review; if unfunded, keep current tax pay.
Continue after **2031** only if two centres renew at covering fees.
After **2031 tax loss**, apply for posted centre-finance work if meetings fail, with written mortgage pay and signed start.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but can test real demand.
S3.quote: I won't call a thank-you a contract.
fieldNote: A **three-centre test** stays within current paid work and requires a supervisor to verify each wage figure.
Two **paid renewals** determine whether meetings remain a salaried task after 2031.

steps.text: Learn monthly pay meetings for three centres with partner funding and supervisor checks
Continue salaried meetings after 2031 only if two centres renew at covering fees
Apply after 2031 loss for posted centre job if meetings fail and written mortgage pay/start fit
Keep paid centre tax files if partner refuses meeting funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets us pay down more mortgage and see what the children choose after school. I would still need a wage at fifty-three, even with a smaller loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask employers to show which work keeps earning a fee and fund learning for staff whose return tasks fade. I'd be wary of a big promise without a named payer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most routine accounts checking to shrink when thinking AI arrives in 2036. The staff-pay meetings might remain useful, but a centre has to budget for them. Robots around 2039 could later change Owen's hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep two hundred monthly going into our reserve while both wages hold and ask the childcare association next spring what paid payroll-liaison roles exist and whether the school rota covers pickup. I would keep our current accounts pay while learning the requirements. In the first year after 2036, if my tax desk closes, I'd seek a newly posted funded liaison role only with written mortgage-covering pay and signed start; otherwise I'd use our reserve and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not overwhelmed. A decade lets us ask who pays for the work before our tax desk disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children contribute by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child might be working by then, but we won't use their pay in the mortgage plan. We would keep building our own reserve while it is possible. I want both children free to choose studies or work without our debt following them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which terms would a liaison post need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the association for the employer's name, posted wage, start date and the actual weekly hours. If there is no vacancy, I stay with paid accounts work while it exists and ask again later. I will not leave for an invitation to network. A current vacancy would not remain open for a decade.

say: I would seek **named payers** for new work before anyone claims it replaces returns.
I would support **funded staff learning** as returns fade.
think: My **routine checks** still shrink in 2036 despite ten years to prepare.
A **liaison post** needs a centre budget to survive.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** while both wages hold.
Check **liaison pay and hours** next spring while keeping current accounts pay.
Seek **posted funded liaison work** after 2036 loss with named employer, written mortgage pay/start and pickup-compatible hours; otherwise use reserve while searching.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about needing wages at fifty-three.
S4.quote: I will not leave for an invitation to network.
fieldNote: A **ten-year runway** supports reserve building without counting the children’s future wages.
A **liaison vacancy** requires employer name, funded salary, signed start and a school-compatible rota.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could stop buying my accounts hours before a new liaison post is funded. A written staffing plan and a posted job with mortgage-covering pay and school-compatible hours would help. Our nine months saved is useful, but it cannot hire me. I need an employer's name beside a vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a worker feels about a corrected pay slip. If a relief worker was shorted, I want someone to explain the correction plainly and own it. A tidy automated answer may still leave a person worried at home.

headlineQuote: Our nine months saved is useful, but it cannot hire me.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Uma prepares childcare-centre accounts and tax returns at Elm Court.
Her **accounting degree** and professional qualification support experienced midlevel work at above-usual pay.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, checking results against signed shift sheets.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and nine months saved give options, with plenty of nearby firms.
She tests **paid staff-pay meetings** and looks for funded centre-liaison work after AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her accounts hours before a funded liaison post exists.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **staffing plan** and a posted, mortgage-covering job with school-compatible hours.
